hero.name: Gaurav Singh

hero.description: I work across React, Next.js, TypeScript, Node.js, NestJS and PostgreSQL, currently on an enterprise freight-forwarding platform at Eagle Inbrit, previously on CometChat's React, Angular and Vue UI Kits and SDK integrations.
about: I've spent the last few years where product UI meets the systems behind it: first on CometChat's developer-facing UI Kits and SDK integrations, now on an enterprise freight-forwarding platform at Eagle Inbrit.

That mix shapes how I work. I think about the API contract and the data model as much as the component, I build reusable pieces that other developers integrate, and I pay attention to the edge cases in long, rule-heavy business workflows.

Alongside that I've designed and built full-stack products across construction, hiring, retail and healthcare, working through permissions, multi-tenant data, approval workflows and reporting on Next.js, NestJS and PostgreSQL.

projects.title: Engineering Workspace
projects.description: An internal platform that brings daily check-ins, task updates, OKRs, performance reviews and peer recognition into one workspace, scoped by organisation, team and role.
projects.tagline: Check-ins, goals, reviews and recognition for engineering teams.
projects.headline: A workspace for engineering organisations to track progress, goals and reviews across teams, without micromanagement.
projects.subheadline: Check-ins, goals, reviews, recognition, and personal work in one workspace.
overview: Engineering leadership runs on two questions: what is actually happening this week, and is anyone blocked. The answers are scattered across a project tracker, a standup thread, a goals document nobody has opened since the quarter started, and a review cycle that arrives twice a year with no supporting evidence.

This workspace collects them. Daily check-ins record progress and blockers. Task updates and personal action items - the follow-ups from Slack, calls, and meetings that never belong in a project tracker - live in each person's workspace. Goals and OKRs run org-wide with progress. Reviews draw on check-ins and recognition that already exist rather than on what a manager can recall.

The dashboard puts it in one place: check-in rate, blockers today, pending reviews, open goals, recognitions this week, average score, check-in activity over time, goal progress across teams, and top contributors. It is built for product companies and engineering organizations large enough that a manager cannot hold the whole picture in their head.

architecture: Multi-organisation data model: organisations contain teams and members, and every check-in, goal, review and recognition is scoped to that hierarchy.
Role-based access control decides who can see and act on what: a member's private workspace, a manager's team view and org-wide goals each have different visibility rules.
Reviews draw on records that already exist (check-ins, goal progress, recognition), so the schema links them rather than duplicating them into the review.
Dashboard metrics (check-in rate, blockers, goal progress, top contributors) are aggregated from the same relational data in PostgreSQL through Prisma.
NestJS modules follow the product domains (check-ins, goals, reviews, recognition, people) behind a REST API consumed by the Next.js app.

projects.title: Construction ERP
projects.description: Projects, procurement, budgets, materials, workforce and site reporting in one system, so a purchase order, a site report and a budget line all trace back to the same project.
projects.headline: A construction management platform connecting site execution, procurement, budgets and workforce for multi-site firms.
projects.subheadline: Projects, procurement, materials, workforce, and finance in one system.
overview: Construction work is coordinated across three places that rarely agree: a site, an office and a supplier's inbox. Purchase orders sit in WhatsApp. Progress lives in a site engineer's notebook. Finance finds out about a cost overrun a month after it happened.

The platform puts the whole chain in one system. A site engineer files a daily report from a phone, and that report attaches to a project. The project holds its own budget, purchase orders, material requests, workforce allocation and documents. When a PO is raised it moves through the firm's approval chain, and committed cost updates against the project budget the moment it clears.

It is designed for firms running multiple active sites with a real procurement function (contractors, real estate developers and infrastructure companies), where vendors, RFQs and approvals need to be tracked against each project.

projects.title: Talent Management
projects.description: Recruitment teams manage jobs, candidates, interviews, emails, and hiring decisions across spreadsheets, email, LinkedIn, and messaging platforms - leading to poor visibility, manual effort, and inconsistent hiring workflows.
projects.tagline: Manage your entire hiring process from job posting to candidate selection.
projects.headline: A talent platform that runs hiring end to end, from job posting to offer.
projects.subheadline: An applicant tracking system with jobs, candidates, pipeline, interviews, mail, and referrals in one workspace.
overview: Recruitment is a coordination problem disguised as a people problem. The job description lives in a doc, applicants arrive by email, screening notes sit in a spreadsheet, interviews are booked from a personal calendar, and referrals are remembered rather than recorded. Every handoff between those tools is a place where a candidate goes quiet and nobody notices.

This foundation puts the whole cycle in one system. A job carries its own applications, pipeline, and hiring team. Candidates move through stages on a board, and every move is written to an activity timeline with who did it and when. Recruitment mail is composed and sent from inside the platform, so correspondence stays attached to the candidate instead of one recruiter's inbox. Employee referrals are a first-class record with their own status, not a forwarded CV.

It is built for HR teams, recruitment agencies, growing startups, and enterprises - anywhere more than one person touches a requisition and leadership eventually asks how the funnel is actually performing. Role and permission management means recruiters, hiring managers, and administrators each see the slice of hiring that belongs to them.

projects.title: Inventory Management
projects.description: Businesses running multiple locations juggle fragmented stock counts, manual billing, and inconsistent GST invoicing - with no single view of what's happening across branches.
projects.tagline: Inventory, barcode billing, and GST - unified.
projects.headline: An inventory and billing foundation for businesses running more than one location.
projects.subheadline: Multi-tenant stock, barcode POS, and GST-compliant invoicing.
overview: Businesses with several shops or warehouses usually end up with several systems. Stock is counted in one place, bills are raised in another, and GST is assembled at the end of the month from whatever the accountant can find. Nobody can answer the simple question - how much of this product do we have, across everything, right now.

This foundation is multi-tenant from the data model up. Each shop is isolated: its own inventory, products, orders, users, and billing. A super admin switches between them from the header and sees the group. Products carry variants, categories, barcodes, minimum stock levels, units, and prices, and inventory is edited in bulk with barcode printing built in.

Billing runs off a barcode scanner in three modes - standard, instant, and raw. CGST and SGST are computed on the line items, your GSTIN prints on the bill, discounts are applied at the sale, and cash or UPI/card is recorded against the order. The GST summary is a screen, not a month-end reconstruction.

projects.title: WhatsApp Clone
projects.description: A cross-platform messaging app for Web, Android, and iOS using Ionic React and CometChat SDK, with a reusable Capacitor push notification plugin.
projects.headline: A full messaging client for web, Android, and iOS built from a single Ionic React codebase.
projects.subheadline: Real-time chat, VoIP calling, reactions, and threaded replies, with the push-notification layer extracted into a Capacitor plugin published on npm.
overview: Messaging looks simple until you ship it to three platforms at once. A browser tab, an Android device, and an iPhone each want a different notification mechanism, a different permission prompt, and a different idea of what happens when a call arrives while the app is closed. Most of the work in a chat client is not the chat.

This app puts the whole surface in one Ionic React codebase and leans on the CometChat SDK for the real-time layer: one-to-one and group conversations, reactions, threaded replies, status updates, and VoIP calls. Capacitor wraps it for the two mobile stores so the same components render natively rather than in a compatibility shim.

The notification handling turned out to be the reusable part. Registering FCM tokens on Android, APNs on iOS, and separate VoIP tokens for incoming calls is the same dance in every Capacitor app, so it was pulled out into its own plugin and published to npm rather than left buried in this project.

projects.title: Clinic Management
projects.description: Clinic websites collect enquiries that go nowhere. Doctors and admins share one login with no clear ownership of a request, and every homepage or services update needs a developer.
projects.tagline: Website enquiries to patient records, connected.
projects.headline: A clinic platform that connects your public website to the people who answer enquiries.
projects.subheadline: Website content, patient enquiries, doctors, and records in one admin.
overview: Most clinic software treats the website and the clinic as two different problems. The website is built by an agency and frozen the day it launches. The enquiry form emails a shared inbox. Nobody owns a request, two people call the same patient, and changing the services list means raising a ticket with whoever built the site.

This foundation makes the website part of the system. Homepage copy, the services catalog, doctor profiles, testimonials, and the statistics strip are edited by your admin from the same panel that manages patient enquiries. An enquiry arrives with the service the patient asked about, gets assigned to a doctor, and moves through New, Viewed, and Completed - so at any moment you can see what came in today and who has not been called back.
It fits multi-location clinics, specialty practices, and telehealth providers: organizations where more than one person handles enquiries, and where the marketing site changes more than once a year.

projects.description: Retail and D2C teams stitch together a storefront, checkout, and staff permissions from separate tools - product data drifts out of sync, checkout breaks under load, and support can't see what the customer sees.

projects.headline: A commerce foundation with a storefront, checkout, and staff admin in one codebase.
projects.subheadline: Catalog, cart, orders, and a full admin with audit logs.
overview: The usual way to launch a store is to rent a platform and pay for every gap in it. A theme here, an app for reviews, another for coupons, a per-seat fee for staff accounts, and a transaction cut forever. It works until your catalog or your workflow stops looking like everyone else's, and then you are extending someone else's product from the outside.

This foundation is the whole thing in one codebase you own. The storefront handles category browsing, search, wishlist, accounts, and cart-to-checkout. The admin behind it manages products with variants and statuses, orders, customers, coupons, reviews, categories, and homepage banners - with audit logs recording who changed what.

It suits D2C brands, multi-category storefronts, and marketplace operators who expect to customize pricing rules, checkout, or fulfilment, and who would rather pay for engineering once than pay a percentage of revenue indefinitely.

projects.subheadline: Services, project record, careers, and enquiries presented for an industrial buyer, with motion and 3D used to carry weight, not decorate.
overview: Industrial contractors are usually sold on credentials: how long you have operated, what you have erected, and whether you can be trusted on a live site. The brief here was to present four decades of structural steel erection work to that audience without the site feeling like a brochure from the same era.

The build pairs a conventional marketing structure (services, project record, careers, contact) with a motion layer that keeps the pages moving under scroll. Framer Motion drives the section reveals and Three.js carries the geometric accents behind the hero, tuned to sit behind the content rather than compete with it.

Credibility markers do the selling: ISO certification, years in operation, and a counted record of completed projects, clients, and installations sit high on the page where an industrial buyer looks for them first.
